Do not reproduce the person in the reference, or any figure, silhouette, reflection of a person or mannequin (brief must_avoid: people).

Do not copy the reference cafe's specific layout (counter plus stool row plus clothing rack plus espresso machine) as a scene. Use it as material evidence, not as a design to replicate.
Avoid recognisable branded objects: espresso machine badges, the CCTV camera, labelled garments.
Cliche risk: sci-fi spaceship or laboratory interior, futuristic robots, chrome 'cyber' styling, glowing neon accents.
Cliche risk: hospital, morgue or operating-room reading of steel plus white light, unless chosen deliberately.
Cliche risk: interior-design or architecture-portfolio advertising shot (lifestyle staging, product props, real-estate wide-angle distortion).
Cliche risk: generic 'AI minimalism' render: plastic-grey CGI steel, perfectly clean surfaces, impossible reflections, floating volumes without contact shadows.
Material-plausibility risk: brushed steel rendered as mirror chrome or as flat grey paint. It must show grain and soft anisotropic sheen.
Imitation risk: do not emulate living artists' signature works (James Turrell skyspaces or Ganzfeld rooms, Anish Kapoor mirror forms, Jeff Koons polished steel, Doug Wheeler infinity environments).
Imitation risk: do not recreate Donald Judd's specific box or stack compositions (estate-controlled oeuvre), or Dan Flavin's fluorescent arrangements.
Imitation risk: do not copy identifiable interiors by living studios (e.g. Creative Studio Unravel's Monoha, Schemata Architects' Blue Bottle Seongsu).
Keep the value range high-key and compressed; dramatic hard shadows or dark moody grading would betray this materiality.

context_notes.note: Brushing creates anisotropic reflection: highlights are stretched into soft streaks perpendicular to the grain, and reflections of the room are blurred rather than mirrored. Under a very large diffuse source (a luminous ceiling) brushed steel goes nearly grey and low in contrast; it is described mainly by the bright line on its top edges, a cooler soft gradient on vertical faces, and faint smudges or fingerprints. In the reference the top surface is the brightest steel plane (it reflects the ceiling), verticals are mid-grey, and the stool tops carry a soft sheen where the sheet is bent.

A backlit opal panel grid or stretched-membrane ceiling turns the light source into a plane. The result is near-shadowless light: only thin contact shadows under objects and a gentle falloff down the walls. It is the light of the gallery, the lab, the clean room and the high-end store. As a cultural form it descends from the modernist ideal of evenly lit, rational space and from Light and Space art, but here in service of display.

O'Doherty's argument that the white, evenly lit gallery removes objects from time and sacralises them applies to minimal retail. A cup, a jug or a folded garment on a steel slab under sourceless light is presented as a relic. Retail and cafe design borrows the gallery's authority; the space becomes the brand.
context_notes.topic: the white cube and retail sacralisation

context_notes.note: Judd's fabricated steel volumes removed the hand and made proportion, edge, interval and surface the content. The reference counter (thick slab on spaced block plinths) and the stools (one bent sheet) inherit this vocabulary as furniture. An artwork can turn this back toward sculpture: the slab as a monolith, its plinths as an interval rhythm, rather than a service counter.

Search snippets indicate that stainless steel interiors have become a recognisable Seoul cafe and retail idiom (Seongsu, Itaewon, Haebangchon), often in former industrial buildings and combined with raw concrete. Snippets cite a cost advantage of stainless in Korea and designers describing an 'aesthetics of absence'. This is context for why the user may find the materiality resonant; it is not something to depict literally.

Han reads the smooth, flawless surface as the aesthetic of consumer capitalism: pleasing, frictionless and without negativity. Tanizaki, from the other side, praises shadow, patina and tarnish. Brushed steel sits between the two. It is industrial and cool, but its grain is a record of abrasion and it marks easily with touch. That ambivalence is the most promising artistic lever.

The reference is almost monochrome: cool white ceiling glow (brightest), warm-grey off-white walls, steel in a mid-grey band with cool highlights, concrete floor slightly darker and warmer, and small black or white accents. Contrast is compressed and there are no deep blacks apart from small accents. Fidelity to this materiality means keeping a narrow, high-key value range.

open_questions: Should the artwork keep an architectural interior (room, ceiling, floor) or isolate a single steel volume against the luminous field?
How much human trace is acceptable under must_avoid 'people': are fingerprints, a used cup or a displaced stool in scope?
Should the luminous ceiling grid appear as a visible structure or only as a light condition reflected in the steel?
Is the intended mood contemplative (gallery or chapel) or critical (sterile commerce)?
Does the pairing with materiality B call for deliberate contrast or kinship between the two works?
interpretation.summary: The user's intent (original text preserved in the brief) announces that two artworks will be made, one from each of two materialities; this brief covers materiality A only. My reading: the task is to turn the reference's material system (brushed stainless steel volumes, a sourceless luminous ceiling, matte white walls and a grey concrete floor) into one autonomous fine-art image, not a reproduction of that cafe. The materiality carries a strong cultural charge. It is the white cube's sacralising light applied to commerce, minimalist sculpture domesticated as furniture, and a current Seoul retail-cafe idiom. The richest artistic territory is the ambivalence of brushed steel under shadowless light. It looks impersonal and frictionless, yet the grain is made by abrasion and the surface records touch. Because people are forbidden, any human dimension must come through traces (smudges, wear, a cup ring, the height and spacing of seats, emptiness after use) or through scale and proportion, never through figures.

tensions.description: Stainless steel is chosen precisely to look untouched and identical, yet it registers every fingerprint and its grain is literally made by repeated abrasion. The person removed from the reference survives only as what the steel retains: a smudge, a cup ring, the polish worn into a stool top. The image must make that absence felt without showing anyone.
tensions.pole_a: human identity as trace (touch, use, waiting, ritual of coffee)
tensions.pole_b: impersonal brushed-steel surface that shows no hand

tensions.description: Diffuse ceiling light removes cast shadows and so removes the usual cues of mass. Heavy steel blocks risk floating as if weightless or reading as CGI. The work has to hold both the immaterial glow and the tonnage of the monolith, mainly through contact shadows, edge highlights and the floor plane.
tensions.pole_a: shadowless, evenly lit sanctity (white cube, Light and Space)
tensions.pole_b: material weight and gravity of the steel volumes

tensions.description: The same vocabulary serves both. Without care the image collapses into an interior-design advertisement. The artwork should pull the material toward sculptural autonomy: no products, no branding, no lifestyle staging.
tensions.pole_b: retail and cafe display (commerce, brand, lifestyle image)

tensions.description: Brushed steel sits between mirror polish and patina. Leaning too far toward the smooth gives a sterile render; leaning too far toward grime betrays the materiality. The productive zone is controlled imperfection: grain, faint marks, a soft gradient.

sources.relevance: The white, evenly lit room is not neutral: it sacralises whatever it contains and in late modernism 'context becomes content'. Directly frames the shadowless white room of the reference as an ideological, quasi-sacred container. URL came from a web search result; the page could not be opened (WebFetch DNS failure), so only the search snippet and model knowledge were used.

sources.relevance: Critique of the frictionless, polished surface (Koons, the iPhone) as the aesthetic of consumer capitalism: the smooth 'does not injure' and offers no resistance. Gives a critical counter-pole to the seductive steel-and-light finish of minimal retail. Known from search snippets of publisher blurbs and model knowledge; book text not opened.
